thread.title: Next, A Real Crash? If So, Why I Would Blame The Fed Most Of All

author: DoctoRx
title: Next, A Real Crash? If So, Why I Would Blame The Fed Most Of All
text:
For three months, it's been better to be fearful than greedy In my December 23 article titled Powell: Let Them Eat Bear , I mentioned that oversold markets that fail to rally are crash-prone. Now we have Apple ( AAPL ) pointing the finger at an economic slowdown in China leading to another decline in the indices, all the while bargain hunters and possibly the US Plunge Protection Team have been trying to get the late year rally extended into something meaningful. I began pointing the finger not only at the Fed but at China when I changed my tone on the markets in October, in Is China Breaking? Some Evidence And Potential Implications . Trying to sort out what's precisely causing what movement in what market is impossible, because everything happens together and controlled experiments are impossible.
Here's why I continue to think that the mainstream and now even the president are missing the main point. As The Hill reports Wednesday:
Trump told reporters Wednesday that the bloody December for U.S. stocks was caused by “a little glitch” and predicted a strong 2019 for the market. He predicted that stocks would rise close to 30 percent by year’s end after the president finalizes trade deals with China and the European Union.
I disagree with that prediction unless the Fed changes its stance immediately.
The article continues:
Trump had frequently blamed the Fed and its chairman, Jerome Powell, for 2018’s rocky market, citing the central bank’s interest rate hikes. He renewed his criticism of the Fed on Wednesday, saying “We need a little help from the Fed,” for the market to rebound, according to Bloomberg .
While traders have braced for rising interest rates driven by Fed rate hikes, analysts have pinned most of the market downturn on trade tensions triggered by Trump’s tariffs on steel, aluminum and Chinese goods. Economists also see growing signs of a global slowdown within the next two years.
As I said on Oct. 15, Yep, The Fed's Going Too Far, And Trump Has A Point: Analysis .
Between that and the China article, with the S&P 500 ( SPY ) around $280, I began the next phase of my frequent prior cautions about how the real elephant in the market's room was the reversal of QE by the Fed (along with the rate hikes). I just do not think that some tariffs, which bring money into the Federal government that reduces its borrowing needs and thus eases financial conditions while allowing the government to assist farmers and others it chooses, can account for more than a 25% drop in regional bank stocks ( KRE ), or a massive bear market in home builder stocks ( ITB ).
Let's look back at the QE era in the US markets. The major bull market from March 2009 to the 2014 peak accounted for almost all the total bull move in the Obama era, and all the up periods in the SPY were related to quantitative easing. QE is a "risk on" tactic. When QE was paused, markets mostly went sideways. Thus:
Is it not logical that reversing QE, and taking what is now $50 B a month, or a massive $0.6 T a year, out of liquidity and into low-yielding bonds, would have the opposite effect on stocks and provide significant headwinds to them?
Yet apparently even now, the focus is on the relevant but non-systemic issue of tariffs.
My view is simple. So long as analysts focus on secondary issues such as tariffs, Brexit and the like - which are clearly important - there may be insufficient focus on the liquidity drain, and a market that is heading down while liquidity is stressed tends to keep heading down. Perhaps even President Trump, who has focused more sharply on the Fed, has taken some mainstream advice and has toned it down, now merely asking for "a little help from the Fed."
I disagree. I think we need a lot of help from the Fed. The Fed could interpret the president's comments as asking for it to not raise rates any further while continuing the relatively unpublicized reversal of QE.
Add in a stock market with above-average valuations and corporations with above-average profit margins, and we have a target. Stocks have beaten bonds, precious metals and cash over the past 10 years. The champion of stocks in the White House looks to be the topic of some nasty impeachment-related testimony from his prior attorney, and who knows what is coming from other witnesses and the Mueller team?
In my 12/23 article, I mentioned that while I was not a big fan of the SPY as a whole, there were several high quality individual stocks that looked attractive without discussing timing. I actually wrote out an entire AAPL article, and when I was finished, I did not submit it because I could not bring myself to re-enter this name given all the China and other risks. I have scaled heavily out of stocks beginning in that October time frame, and writing on the Internet involves thinking of being timely, not just saying that I like something well-known over the next decade relative to today's low interest rates.
For now, I know my position, which remains risk-off while the Fed fiddles around with its models while much is getting scary out there.
To add a little more perspective, I believe that what makes alpha is finding a theme that is valid and undiscovered or insufficiently so. When I began writing on the Internet a decade ago, I thought that theme was that with QE rampant and with deflation worries abounding, precious metals and other hard assets were likely to move to or toward all-time highs given the massive QE (now called QE 1). Later, in Q2 2011, I did a 180 degree reversal and went heavily for bonds on the theme that silver ( SLV ) near $40 was loony, and so on, given that QE 2 had ended. Not all my ideas work out as well as those two, so I'm not claiming anything close to genius or super-lucky status. However, when something does appear to work, as the liquidity drain hypothesis appears to me to be explaining a lot, I stick with it until it either becomes popular or is disproven.
Before I sum up, please remember that:
I am a long-only investor; I'm not wishing for bad times I'm trying to provide information and ideas for you to consider, not trying to get you to make any specific financial or other decisions. Concluding remarks - staying safe (with an indeterminate time frame) while economies downshift and central banks withdraw liquidity In the Dec. 23 article, I mentioned that a Ned Davis Research model assigns about a 90% chance that the world is in an OECD-defined recession or about to be in one. Given that as a real possibility, and remembering that recessions begin by definition at the top of an economic wave, I find the combination of 9 rate hikes by the Fed, the ending of QE this week by the European Central Bank, and especially the lack of financial media focus on the liquidity drain more major than is thought. All the "known knowns" such as trade wars, Brexit and possible impeachment (on grounds yet unknown) of the president are not positives, either. Add to that broken-down charts of all the major averages, and who is going to aggressively buy the dip? And with what liquidity until the Fed injects more? Thus, why not sell to the Plunge Protection Team if it is in the market one way or another?
Now, it's important to emphasize there is no certainty here of what the Fed will do and how the US and global economies will go. Even if my very cautious views on risk assets prove valid for a while, they may not do so in any specific time frame. I was very bearish on crude oil-related stocks in an April article , but it took a while for the oil market to agree with me. It's important to be patient with a thesis. Yet I do think there is reason to fear something cracking worse in the stock market than has already occurred, and to respect the sharp downtrend and continue to play it safe.
AAPL pointed to weakness in China's smartphone market not being limited to the iPhone; China is now an important cog in the global economic machine. I suspect that what happens in China does not stay there.
I have been speaking well of bonds for some months as the flip side of my concerns about monetary deflation caused by the Fed. I'm staying long Treasuries ( TLT ) as well as other high-quality fixed income and extra cash. 2018 had a bull market in cash, and while that may continue for a while, Treasuries now have some momentum (but may have moved too far too fast in the short run).
As far as the question in the title goes, yes, I fear one sooner rather than later. I think it's getting late in the day for the Fed to see what I view as its policy error, and (yikes) the ECB is now withdrawing liquidity, too.
Thanks for reading and sharing any thoughts you wish to contribute. Note, I might be forced to hit the road tomorrow and may have limited Internet access for a while if that happens. So if I do not comment on the article, you know why.
Good luck to us all.
Submitted Wednesday night, S&P futures 2479, 10-year Treasury 2.62%.
